subject: Whats a reasonable sampling time for a IRT model?

messages.author: 71bfb5f1e96782a8
messages.subject: Whats a reasonable sampling time for a IRT model?
parts:
Hi,

i use an IRT model to analyze data from about 450 people answering 3 questionnaires (overall 40 items) at the same time with stan. I assume different, but correlated latent abilities for each questionnaire. Sampling 10,000 iterations takes about 4-5 hrs on my regular desktop pc. is this a reasonable duration or would you think there is something off?

Best, Felix

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Whats a reasonable sampling time for a IRT model?
parts:
Hi Felix,

It's really hard to answer that. How fast does it run on simulated data? If it's the same order of magnitude, then it's reasonable. If it's not, then the model may not be as appropriate for your data as you might have imagined. Also, before doing that, check the n_eff first.

Question: why do you run 10,000 iterations? Iterations is not equal to effective sample size.


Daniel

messages.author: 71bfb5f1e96782a8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Whats a reasonable sampling time for a IRT model?
parts:
Thanks, that makes sense. I'll attach the model below. Data is in the long format and i have a different number of categories per item, that made it a bit difficult. The main purpose of the model is not to estimate item parameters from scratch, but use existing parameters for these questionnaires as a prior and update those given new data.

Effective sample size is between 100 and 2000, depending on the parameter. Is there any guideline what i should have?

Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
97.68 1165.00 1680.00 1532.00 1987.00 2250.00 


data{
  int P;                       //nr items
  int N;                       //nr persons
  
  int Number_of_responses;
  int Categories[P];           //nr categories per item -1
  int Borders[P+1];           // to know which parameter belongs to which item
  
  int Questionnaire[Number_of_responses]; //current questionnaire
  int ID[Number_of_responses];//current id
  int Item[Number_of_responses]; //current item

  int Response[Number_of_responses]; // actual response
  
  vector[P] prior_alpha;                //prior information on slope
  vector[sum(Categories)] prior_kappa; //prior information on thresholds
  
  real prior_sd; //overall prior sd
}

parameters {
  vector[sum(Categories)] kappa;              // intercepts
  vector<lower=0>[P] alpha;                   // slope
  vector[3] Means;                            //latent variable means
  
  matrix[N, 3] theta;         //questionnaire specific abilities for each person
  
  cov_matrix[3] sigma;        //covariance between abilities
  
}

transformed parameters{
  vector[sum(Categories)] kappa_star;              // intercepts
  vector[Number_of_responses] theta_star;           // ability in long format
  
  
  
  for (i in 1:P){
    kappa_star[(Borders[i]+1):Borders[i+1]] = (-1) * sort_desc(kappa[(Borders[i]+1):Borders[i+1]]);
  }
  
  
  for (n in 1:Number_of_responses){
    if (Questionnaire[n] == 1) theta_star[n] = theta[ID[n],1];
    if (Questionnaire[n] == 2) theta_star[n] = theta[ID[n],2];
    if (Questionnaire[n] == 3) theta_star[n] = theta[ID[n],3];
  }
}


model {
  Means ~ normal(0,1);

  for (i in 1:N) theta[i,] ~ multi_normal(Means, sigma);

  alpha ~ normal(prior_alpha , prior_sd);
  kappa ~ normal(prior_kappa, prior_sd);
  
  
  for (n in 1:Number_of_responses){
    Response[n] ~ ordered_logistic(theta_star[n]* alpha[Item[n]], kappa_star[(Borders[Item[n]]+1):Borders[Item[n]+1]]);
    
  }
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Whats a reasonable sampling time for a IRT model?
parts:
I'm afraid we don't have vectorization for these graded IRT models.

There aren't any guidelines in general because everything varies
by model, match of data to the model, and the way it's all coded
as a Stan program.

But the big thing you want to do for speed is to (1) replace that
covariance matrix data structure with a Cholesky factor, and (2) vectorize.
For (1), we recommend a scaled correlation matrix (see the manual chapter on
regression for an example), but you can also use just a covariance
matrix Cholesky factor. Given that have an improper prior on the
covariance matrix, you'll get the same result. For (2), you need to
put the observations into an array of vectors. You'll need:


vector[3] theta[N];

as the data type, then you can just do

theta ~ multi_normal_cholesky(means, L_cov);

- Bob
